entry.authors: Cennamo, C., Kretschmer, T., Constantiou, I. & Garcés, E. (LAMA Economic Research, for CCIA Europe)
entry.title: Economic Impact of the Digital Markets Act on European Businesses and the European Economy
entry.method: calculation: revenue-loss rates taken from published studies of reduced personalisation, reach and integration, applied to Eurostat B2C web sales of firms that use online advertising, by sector and country; no measured post-DMA outcomes
entry.outcomes: business revenue and revenue per worker in EU service sectors
entry.headline: Estimates that DMA-driven loss of platform efficiency could cost EU businesses in the sectors covered EUR 8.5bn to EUR 114bn in revenue (0.05%-0.64% of turnover), up to EUR 1,122 per worker a year; accommodation EUR 1-14bn, retail EUR 4.4-59bn.
entry.summary_plain: An industry-funded study calculates that the DMA's limits on how gatekeepers personalise ads, rank results and combine services could cost European businesses up to EUR 114bn a year in lost sales.
entry.quality: Projection, not a measurement: loss rates are assumed from other studies rather than observed after the DMA; upper bound depends on how intensively firms use platform tools; funded by CCIA Europe.
entry.verified: full text read (executive summary and methodology)
entry.interested_party: Funded by CCIA Europe (trade association whose members include gatekeepers); academic authors received a grant from LAMA Economic Research
entry.citation: Cennamo, C., Kretschmer, T., Constantiou, I. & Garcés, E. (LAMA Economic Research, for CCIA Europe) (2025), Economic Impact of the Digital Markets Act on European Businesses and the European Economy, LAMA Economic Research report, June 2025

entry.authors: Belafatti, F., Bergmanis-Korāts, G., Haiduchyk, T., Khusnutdinov, M., Kubś, J. & Šuminas, A. (NATO StratCom COE)
entry.title: Impact of the Digital Services Act: A Facebook Case Study
entry.venue: NATO Strategic Communications Centre of Excellence, Riga, May 2025
entry.method: before/after comparison of harmful posts by Polish and Lithuanian Facebook accounts in 2023 and 2024; posts flagged by GPT-4o mini and validated by larger language models (959 harmful posts in 2023, 1,392 in 2024); availability of posts checked in November 2024
entry.outcomes: prevalence of harmful content (mainly hate speech), fact-checking, removal of harmful posts
entry.headline: Harmful posts rose 45% from 2023 to 2024 (+55% in Polish, -11% in Lithuanian); about 90% were hate speech. Fact-checked posts rose 45%, but the share of harmful posts removed fell from 12% to 4% (Lithuanian 33.3% to 0.8%; Polish 11% to 4.5%). The authors could not find an overall improvement after DSA enforcement.
entry.summary_plain: A NATO-affiliated study of Polish and Lithuanian Facebook found more hate speech and fewer removals in 2024 than in 2023, despite the DSA, though Facebook did more fact-checking.
entry.quality: Simple before/after comparison with no control group; AI classification (accuracy reported in an appendix); 2024 posts had less time to be removed than 2023 posts; two small language markets only.
entry.verified: full text read (executive summary, removal and conclusions sections)
entry.citation: Belafatti, F., Bergmanis-Korāts, G., Haiduchyk, T., Khusnutdinov, M., Kubś, J. & Šuminas, A. (NATO StratCom COE) (2025), Impact of the Digital Services Act: A Facebook Case Study, NATO Strategic Communications Centre of Excellence, Riga, May 2025

entry.title: The Competitive Effects of the GDPR
entry.method: economic and legal analysis (conceptual); no data of its own
entry.outcomes: competition and concentration in data markets, data sharing
entry.headline: Argues the GDPR limits competition in data-driven markets and favours more concentrated market structures by restricting data collection and sharing; identifies seven market dynamics behind these unintended effects and proposes remedies (less legal uncertainty, certification, data-sharing duties).
entry.summary_plain: Two law professors argue that the GDPR, while protecting privacy, tends to help large data holders and make markets more concentrated.
entry.quality: Conceptual; cites early empirical evidence but does not test its claims.
entry.verified: abstract and part of the full text read
entry.citation: Gal, M. S. & Aviv, O. (2020), The Competitive Effects of the GDPR, Journal of Competition Law & Economics 16(3), 349-391

entry.authors: Tianshu Sun, Zhe Yuan, Chunxiao Li, Kaifu Zhang and Jun Xu
entry.title: The Value of Personal Data in Internet Commerce: A High-Stakes Field Experiment on Data Regulation Policy
entry.method: Randomised field experiment: for 555,800 customers, personal data were removed from the home-page recommendation algorithm, simulating a data-use restriction; outcomes compared with a control group
entry.finding: Without personal data, recommendations became markedly more concentrated on fewer products and matching outcomes fell sharply: lower click-through, browsing, sales volume and sales amount. The losses were larger for niche merchants and for customers who gain most from e-commerce.
entry.summary_plain: When Alibaba switched off personal data in its recommendations for half a million shoppers, they bought much less and small sellers lost most, suggesting rules that restrict personalisation have real costs.
entry.relevance: Tests the kind of restriction on personal data use for personalised recommendation found in the GDPR and in the DMA's and DSA's limits on profiling.
entry.caveats: A simulated ban in China, not an evaluation of an EU law; short-run effects on one platform; three co-authors work at Alibaba.
entry.interested_party: Three co-authors employed by Alibaba Group
